Fit a conductance model by maximum likelihood

Source: R/radish_optimize.R
terradish.Rd

Uses maximum likelihood to fit a parameterized conductance surface to genetic data, given a function relating spatial data to conductance (a "conductance model") and a function linking the graph kernel to an observed genetic distance or covariance matrix (a "measurement model").

Usage

terradish(
  formula,
  data,
  conductance_model = loglinear_conductance,
  measurement_model = mlpe,
  nu = NULL,
  theta = NULL,
  leverage = FALSE,
  nonnegative = TRUE,
  conductance = TRUE,
  optimizer = c("newton", "bfgs", "auto"),
  verbose = FALSE,
  control = NewtonRaphsonControl(ctol = 1e-06, ftol = 1e-06),
  validate = FALSE,
  cores = 1L,
  curvature = c("exact", "gauss_newton"),
  solver = c("direct", "auto", "amg"),
  solver_control = NULL,
  approximation = c("none", "landmark", "coarse_raster"),
  approximation_control = NULL,
  measurement_control = NULL,
  slim = FALSE
)

Arguments

formula

A formula with an observed genetic distance or covariance matrix on the left-hand side and conductance covariates from data on the right-hand side.

data

An object of class terradish_graph (see conductance_surface)

conductance_model

A function of class terradish_conductance_model_factory (see terradish_conductance_model_factory)

measurement_model

A function of class terradish_measurement_model (see terradish_measurement_model)

nu

Effective Wishart degrees of freedom passed to measurement models that require it, such as generalized_wishart and wishart_covariance. It must be supplied and is not estimated. It controls effective information, not a marker count. Report sensitivity across plausible values with terradish_rescale_nu. Ignored by non-Wishart measurement models.

theta

Optional starting values for the conductance parameters, on the scale reported by coef() (log conductance per unit of each covariate; map units for Gaussian sigma.<layer> terms) and in the order of the model terms. The default NULL uses the conductance model's default start, which is zero for every log-linear coefficient.

leverage

Logical. Compute leverage (influence) arrays? When TRUE, the fit stores leverage$S, a focal-site by focal-site by parameter array giving the first-order change in each conductance estimate per unit change in each entry of the response matrix, and leverage$X, the corresponding array for the spatial covariates (the change in each estimate per unit change in a covariate value at a graph vertex). Large absolute values flag observations or cells that drive an estimate. Unavailable for Gaussian scale-aware models.

nonnegative

Force regression-like measurement_model to have nonnegative slope?

conductance

Retained for backward compatibility. Only conductance = TRUE is currently implemented.

optimizer

The optimization algorithm to use: newton uses the exact Hessian during optimization, with computational cost that grows linearly with the number of parameters; bfgs uses an approximate Hessian during optimization with cheaper iterations but often more steps; and auto selects bfgs when there are more than three conductance parameters and newton otherwise, unless the conductance model declares a preferred optimizer (the Gaussian scale-aware model always prefers bfgs). Regardless of the optimizer, terradish() evaluates the fitted model once more at the final parameter values using the requested curvature, so standard errors and summaries use the selected final derivative machinery.

verbose

Logical. Should the optimizer report its progress? The default FALSE fits silently. Set TRUE to see the iteration count, objective value, gradient norm, and Hessian determinant at each step, which is what you want when a fit fails to converge or you are tuning control. The trace is emitted with message(), so you can also capture or silence it with suppressMessages(). Setting verbose explicitly overrides the verbose field of control; leaving it alone lets a hand-built control object speak for itself. The much noisier line-search trace stays separate: turn it on with control = NewtonRaphsonControl(ls.control = HagerZhangControl(verbose = TRUE)).

control

A list containing options for the optimization routine (see NewtonRaphsonControl for list)

validate

Reserved. Numerical validation of leverage is not currently implemented in terradish(): validate = TRUE is ignored with a warning. Leave at FALSE.

cores

Number of worker processes. 1 evaluates serially. Parallel execution is experimental and uses PSOCK workers on every operating system. Only Hessian and partial solves run in parallel; AMG and cached CHOLMOD ignore this setting. Multiple workers can be slower on small graphs. A one-time message explains these limits when applicable. On Windows, one PSOCK cluster is retained for the duration of the fit instead of being rebuilt for every derivative evaluation.

curvature

Curvature used for optimization steps and for the returned covariance matrix. "exact" (default) uses the exact Hessian. "gauss_newton" uses an information-based approximation that drops residual-weighted second-derivative terms and requires only first derivatives of the conductance model. It equals the exact Hessian only when those omitted terms are zero or negligible; convergence alone does not guarantee agreement. Standard errors from summary() are then the asymptotic information-based errors. With leverage = TRUE the leverage diagnostics inherit the same approximation.

solver

Linear-system solver. "direct" uses sparse Cholesky, "amg" uses algebraic multigrid, and "auto" chooses AMG above the large-graph threshold regardless of the number of right-hand sides. AMG iteration counts can rise with conductance contrast.

solver_control

Optional named list of solver settings passed to terradish_algorithm. For solver = "direct", supported entries include factorization, supernodal_min_vertices, supernodal_max_rhs, perm, and solve_backend; the latter can be "matrix" or the experimental "cholmod_cpp" and "cholmod_cpp_cached" backends. reference = "auto" grounds a maximum-conductance vertex on high-contrast graphs; "last" retains the original reference. This changes the numerical solve while preserving the same graph model. Direct solves also reject relative system residuals exceeding residual_tolerance = 1e-8; see terradish_algorithm. For solver = "auto", supported selection entries include auto_direct_max_vertices, auto_amg_min_vertices. The legacy auto_direct_max_rhs setting is accepted but no longer affects selection. For solver = "amg" or "auto", terradish() also understands an adaptive schedule with entries such as adaptive, tol_early, tol_mid, tol_final, maxit_early, maxit_mid, maxit_final, and warmup_evals. AMG controls also support reuse_preconditioner to reuse multigrid hierarchy information across nearby optimization steps when possible, and reuse_preconditioner_max_age to periodically rebuild a reused hierarchy. Direct supernodal factorizations can benefit from a threaded BLAS, but those thread counts are controlled by the external R/BLAS build rather than by terradish() itself. If a fit stops with a CHOLMOD or non-positive-definite reduced Laplacian message, the current conductance values made the graph numerically singular. Common fixes are to scale raster covariates, start conductance parameters closer to zero, check retained raster cells for missing or infinite values, and retry with solver = "auto" or solver = "amg" while diagnosing the problem.

approximation

Exploratory approximation used during optimization. "none" uses the full focal set throughout. "landmark" optimizes first on a space-filling subset of focal populations and then refines on the full likelihood when supported by the measurement model. "coarse_raster" optimizes first on an aggregated raster and then refines on the full-resolution graph. If multiple coarse factors are supplied, they are evaluated from coarsest to finest before the final full-resolution stage. This is an opt-in warm-start strategy, not a replacement for the exact full-resolution likelihood. Exact refinement is required.

approximation_control

Optional named list controlling the landmark or coarse-raster approximation. Landmark entries include n_landmarks, fraction, min_landmarks, max_landmarks, method ("spacefill", "random", or "sequential"), seed, and exact_refine. For approximation = "coarse_raster", supported entries include factor, aggregate_fun, directions, exact_refine, and refine_control; this path requires conductance_surface(..., saveStack = TRUE). factor may be a single positive integer or a vector such as c(8, 4, 2) for a multilevel coarse-to-fine warm start. The final reported fit is still evaluated on the full data. refine_control may be a NewtonRaphsonControl list used only for that final exact full-resolution refinement; by default the main control is reused. For measurement_model = leastsquares, landmark exact-refinement is guarded and the approximation stage is skipped.

measurement_control

Optional NewtonRaphsonControl object for the inner nuisance-parameter profile. This is separate from control, which governs optimization of the conductance parameters. The fitted object records the inner optimizer's convergence code and iteration count for the final evaluation. A failed nuisance warm start is retried from the model's default start, retaining any fixed values and custom bounds. Warnings from the failed attempt remain visible; the retry is accepted only if it converges. Standard MLPE nuisance fits scale the resistance slope internally; their convergence criterion is therefore independent of resistance units.

slim

Logical. If TRUE, apply slim_terradish to the returned fit, removing model closures and leverage arrays. Use this for durable storage only when later conductance prediction and model reevaluation are unnecessary.

Value

An object of class c("terradish", "radish"), a list. Most users need only the methods: summary() for estimates, standard errors, and nuisance-parameter intervals, coef() and confint() for conductance coefficients, conductance() and plot() for maps and curves, and AIC(), anova(), or aic_table for comparison (see terradish_methods). The list elements are:

call, formula

The matched call and the model formula.

dim

Named vector with the number of graph vertices (raster cells), focal sites, and graph edges.

convergence

List describing the conductance optimization: code (0 converged, 1 iteration limit reached, 2 stalled or line search failed), message, iterations, max_abs_projected_gradient, criterion, boundary (TRUE when an estimate sits on a bound or no resistance structure was detected), and restarted. Check object$convergence$code == 0 before interpreting estimates.

fit

The final graph and likelihood evaluation. object$fit$phi holds the nuisance (measurement-model) estimates on the measurement model's internal scale, for example log precision; summary() reports them with intervals. object$fit$fitted is the expected response matrix among focal sites. object$fit$subproblem$convergence is the nuisance optimizer's code (0 means converged), which should also be 0 before estimates are interpreted.

loglik, df, aic

Maximized log-likelihood, number of estimated parameters (conductance coefficients plus nuisance parameters), and \(AIC = -2\ell + 2K\).

mle

Conductance estimates (theta, on the log-conductance scale per unit of each covariate as supplied to the graph), and the gradient and Hessian of the log-likelihood at the estimate. Elements ending in _internal are on the optimizer's scale.

submodels

The conductance-model and measurement-model functions used for the fit; conductance() and plot() reuse them.

comparison

Measurement family, nu, graph fingerprint, and response columns that aic_table and anova() use to check that fits are comparable.

cost, diagnostics, approximation

Newton steps and function calls, solver timing and evaluation diagnostics, and a record of any landmark or coarse-raster warm start.

gaussian_scale_info, spline_monotonicity

Metadata for Gaussian smoothing and spline conductance terms, or NULL.

leverage

Leverage arrays for the response (S) and spatial covariates (X) when leverage = TRUE, otherwise NULL entries.

storage

Present only when slim = TRUE; records the model closures and leverage arrays that were removed.

Details

A parameterized conductance surface maps raster covariates to positive vertex conductance. Vertex values define weighted edges and a graph Laplacian \(L(\theta)\). Its generalized inverse \(E(\theta) = L(\theta)^+\) is the shared graph-process kernel. Distance likelihoods use resistance distances derived from \(E(\theta)\), whereas covariance likelihoods use the kernel directly. The selected probability model is called the measurement model. These alternatives describe how related genetic summaries are observed; they are not competing biological process theories.

For example, a log-linear choice of conductance model is:

vertex_conductance[i] = exp(covariates[i,] %*% theta)

where theta are unknown parameters, covariates is a design matrix with each row representing a vertex in the graph (cell in the raster). The conductance of a given edge (an off-diagonal entry in the graph Laplacian) is:

edge_conductance[i,j] = vertex_conductance[i] + vertex_conductance[j]

if argument conductance = TRUE, and

edge_conductance[i,j] = 1/(1/vertex_conductance[i] + 1/vertex_conductance[j])

otherwise. This alternative parameterization is not currently implemented, so conductance must be TRUE. This differs by a factor of two from CIRCUITSCAPE, where the edge conductance/resistance is the average of the vertex conductance/resistance.

terradish estimates theta by maximizing the selected measurement likelihood for the observed response. The optimization is done via Newton's method (default; requires computation of Hessian during optimization), via the BFGS algorithm (requires gradient only during optimization) if optimizer = "bfgs", or via a simple parameter-count heuristic if optimizer = "auto". Fitting one parameterized surface to the genetic data, instead of regressing on separately computed resistance distances, follows Peterman and Pope (2021). In all cases, the final returned fit is evaluated at the optimized parameters using the requested curvature for inference.

Conductance coefficients are conditional model associations. Their sign and magnitude depend on covariate coding, other terms, graph construction, response, measurement likelihood, and candidate set. They are not direct estimates of causal effects, habitat suitability, migration, dispersal, or organismal movement rates.

For an explanation of how categorical spatial covariates are handled, see details of conductance_surface and the examples below. The dummy coding of categorical covariates is done by the function passed to conductance_model (e.g. terradish::loglinear_conductance).

Large rasters. For large continuous rasters, two opt-in helpers can reduce runtime. First, build the graph with conductance_surface(..., crop_buffer = ) when focal sites occupy only part of the raster. This removes vertices outside the buffered sampling extent before fitting. Cropping changes resistance: an unpublished development check on one landscape found increases of 15–23% with a two-cell buffer and 1–2% with a ten-cell buffer. These values are case-specific. Refit with a larger buffer to assess sensitivity on your landscape. Second, use approximation = "coarse_raster" with approximation_control = list(factor = c(4, 2), exact_refine = TRUE) to optimize on one or more aggregated rasters before refining on the original graph. With exact_refine = TRUE, the returned coefficients and likelihood are from the full-resolution graph; the coarse fits are only starting values. To keep the full-resolution cleanup deliberately short, pass refine_control = NewtonRaphsonControl(maxit = 2, ...) inside approximation_control. Exact refinement is required.

For spline terms, summary() reports monotonicity over the covariate range at the focal sites, including the number of derivative sign changes. A monotone curve increases or decreases throughout that range; a nonmonotone curve changes direction. This describes the fitted curve, not a confidence statement about its shape outside or within that range.

Gaussian scale-aware conductance. gaussian_smoothed_loglinear_conductance can also use approximation = "coarse_raster". In that case the Gaussian smoother is rebuilt on each aggregated raster, while the full-resolution sigma bounds and unit conversion are preserved so a warm-started sigma continues to mean the same map-unit distance at every stage.

Currently, all of the built-in conductance models in terradish use the default contrast coding (e.g. for a categorical covariate with K factors, the estimated parameters are the K-1 mean differences against a reference category). The intercept is excluded if it is not identifiable.

If the resistance contribution is zero, or the formula specifies uniform conductance, conductance coefficients are not identified and their influence, gradient, and Hessian are unavailable. A zero environmental kernel weight does not by itself remove conductance inference.

Convergence and starting values. Inspect fit$convergence before interpreting estimates. Code 0 requires a largest absolute projected gradient below ctol, or an objective change below ftol together with a projected gradient below sqrt(ctol). Code 1 means the iteration limit was reached; code 2 means a stall or failed line search. The projected gradient ignores components pointing outside active parameter bounds. The record includes the criterion, iterations, gradient, boundary status, and whether a restart was attempted. A small objective change alone is not convergence. Also inspect fit$fit$subproblem$convergence for nuisance optimization. Numerical convergence does not establish model adequacy.

If a user-supplied starting point reaches a no-structure boundary, fitting retries the default starting point and keeps the better likelihood. Report starting-value sensitivity when distinct solutions remain plausible.

Effective Wishart information

For Wishart likelihoods, nu scales the log likelihood. Point estimates do not depend on it, but standard errors, likelihood-ratio tests, and information criteria do. It is a dispersion parameter that you set, rather than the number of markers. Linkage and the population history shared by loci can make effective information much smaller than the SNP count. In unpublished forward-time simulations run during development, standard errors at the SNP count were three to five times smaller than the spread among replicate histories. Those model-based errors understated uncertainty.

Use terradish_cv_folds to compare conductance formulas, and terradish_rescale_nu to report inference across plausible values. For the same successful folds and nuisance settings, changing nu rescales Wishart CV scores without changing their ranking. Neither procedure identifies the true effective information or repairs an unsuitable response matrix.

References

Peterman WE, Pope NS (2021). The use and misuse of regression models in landscape genetic analyses. Molecular Ecology, 30, 37–47. doi:10.1111/mec.15716 .

Clarke RT, Rothery P, Raybould AF (2002). Confidence limits for regression relationships between distance matrices: estimating gene flow with distance. Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics, 7, 361–372. doi:10.1198/108571102320 .

Hanks EM, Hooten MB (2013). Circuit theory and model-based inference for landscape connectivity. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 108, 22–33. doi:10.1080/01621459.2012.724647 .

See also

conductance_surface to build data, terradish_methods and terradish_inference to read a fit, terradish_conductance_model_factory and terradish_measurement_model for the model choices.

Other model fitting: conductance(), terradish_algorithm(), terradish_distance(), terradish_grid(), terradish_methods

Examples

# \donttest{
library(terra)

data(melip)
covariates <- c(terra::unwrap(melip.altitude),
                terra::unwrap(melip.forestcover))
coords <- terra::unwrap(melip.coords)

# Name the layers first, then scale them. Scaling avoids numeric overflow
# and makes each coefficient a per-standard-deviation effect.
names(covariates) <- c("altitude", "forestcover")
covariates <- scale_covariates(covariates)

# A few melip sites share a raster cell; keep one site per cell.
keep <- !duplicated(terra::cellFromXY(covariates, terra::crds(coords)))
coords <- coords[keep]
Fst <- melip.Fst[keep, keep]

# Build the graph (eight neighbors by default).
surface <- conductance_surface(covariates, coords)

# MLPE (the default) accounts for pairs that share a sampling site.
fit_mlpe <- terradish(Fst ~ altitude + forestcover, data = surface,
                      measurement_model = mlpe)
fit_mlpe$convergence$code   # 0 means converged; check before reading on
#> [1] 0
summary(fit_mlpe)
#> Conductance surface with 22443 vertices (34 focal) estimated by maximum likelihood
#> Call:   terradish(formula = Fst ~ altitude + forestcover, data = surface, 
#>     measurement_model = mlpe)
#> 
#> Loglikelihood: 1825.936 (6 degrees freedom)
#> AIC: -3639.873 
#> 
#> Number of function calls: 22 
#> Number of optimization steps: 6 
#> Convergence: converged | projected gradient: 4.82e-08 
#> Norm of gradient at MLE: 6.341795e-08 
#> 
#> Nuisance parameters (conditional on fitted conductance surface; measurement-model scale):
#>        Estimate  Std. Error  Lower 95%  Upper 95%
#> alpha  -0.04170   0.00853    -0.05842   -0.02498 
#> beta    0.33838   0.01138     0.31608    0.36068 
#> tau     6.64870   0.16712     6.32116    6.97625 
#> rho     0.65243   0.26065     0.14157    1.16330 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> altitude    -0.40667    0.06327  -6.428  1.3e-10 ***
#> forestcover  0.20608    0.10103   2.040   0.0414 *  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Correlation of Coefficients:
#>             altitude
#> forestcover 0.167607
exp(coef(fit_mlpe))         # conductance multiplier per one SD
#>    altitude forestcover 
#>   0.6658661   1.2288485 

# Least squares ignores shared-site dependence; useful for exploration.
fit_ls <- terradish(Fst ~ altitude + forestcover, data = surface,
                    measurement_model = leastsquares)

# Conductance surface with a 95% pointwise interval
fitted_conductance <- conductance(surface, fit_mlpe, quantile = 0.95)

# Test for an interaction using a likelihood-ratio test
fit_mlpe_interaction <- terradish(Fst ~ forestcover * altitude,
                                  data = surface, measurement_model = mlpe)
anova(fit_mlpe, fit_mlpe_interaction)
#> Likelihood ratio test: chi-square (1 df)
#> Null: ~ altitude + forestcover
#> Alt: ~ forestcover + altitude + forestcover:altitude
#>      logLik Df  ChiSq Df(ChiSq)  Pr(>Chi)    
#> Null 1825.9  6                               
#> Alt  1839.8  7 27.627         1 1.471e-07 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Test against the uniform-conductance (isolation by distance) model
fit_mlpe_ibd <- terradish(Fst ~ 1, data = surface, measurement_model = mlpe)
anova(fit_mlpe, fit_mlpe_ibd)
#> Likelihood ratio test: chi-square (2 df)
#> Null: ~ 1
#> Alt: ~ altitude + forestcover
#>      logLik Df  ChiSq Df(ChiSq)  Pr(>Chi)    
#> Null 1783.4  4                               
#> Alt  1825.9  6 85.133         2 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Categorical covariates must be factor-valued layers; see the Details of
# ?conductance_surface.
forestcover <- terra::unwrap(melip.forestcover)
forestcover_class <- cut(terra::values(forestcover)[, 1],
                         breaks = c(0, 1/6, 1/3, 1))
forestcover_cat <- terra::setValues(forestcover,
                                    as.numeric(forestcover_class))
forestcover_cat <- terra::as.factor(forestcover_cat)
RAT <- levels(forestcover_cat)[[1]]
RAT$VALUE <- levels(forestcover_class) # explicitly define level names
levels(forestcover_cat) <- RAT

covariates_cat <- c(forestcover_cat, covariates[["altitude"]])
names(covariates_cat) <- c("forestcover", "altitude")
surface_cat <- conductance_surface(covariates_cat, coords)

# Coefficients for forestcover are contrasts against the first class.
fit_mlpe_cat <- terradish(Fst ~ forestcover + altitude, surface_cat,
                          measurement_model = mlpe)
summary(fit_mlpe_cat)
#> Conductance surface with 22443 vertices (34 focal) estimated by maximum likelihood
#> Call:   terradish(formula = Fst ~ forestcover + altitude, data = surface_cat, 
#>     measurement_model = mlpe)
#> 
#> Loglikelihood: 1824.911 (6 degrees freedom)
#> AIC: -3637.823 
#> 
#> Number of function calls: 22 
#> Number of optimization steps: 6 
#> Convergence: converged | projected gradient: 9.35e-08 
#> Norm of gradient at MLE: 1.010877e-07 
#> 
#> Nuisance parameters (conditional on fitted conductance surface; measurement-model scale):
#>        Estimate   Std. Error  Lower 95%  Upper 95%
#> alpha  -0.042416   0.008777   -0.059619  -0.025212
#> beta    0.474134   0.015981    0.442813   0.505456
#> tau     6.598406   0.171054    6.263146   6.933665
#> rho     0.729229   0.260313    0.219026   1.239433
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> forestcover   0.2105     0.1447   1.455    0.146    
#> altitude     -0.4231     0.0634  -6.674 2.49e-11 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
